lessons.summary: Turn an interest into a feasible learning goal, product goal and evidence plan.
objectives: Separate learning and product goals.
Define meaningful success criteria.
Plan evidence of process and reflection.
keyIdeas: The learning goal describes what the learner will understand or become able to do.
The product goal describes what will be created or performed.
Success criteria should be testable before production begins.

definitions.meaning: The knowledge or skill the learner intends to develop.
The intended outcome, artefact or performance.
Dated records showing decisions, research, action, feedback and change.

method: Name the interest and intended learning.
Define a product that can demonstrate the learning.
Set measurable quality criteria.
Plan milestones, evidence and feedback points.

workedExample.prompt: Improve “I want to make an app about recycling.”
steps: Learning goal: learn to design and test accessible information architecture.
Product goal: create a working prototype for local recycling decisions.
Criteria: users complete three sorting tasks accurately; text works at 200% zoom; content sources are recorded.
workedExample.conclusion: The revised goals distinguish learning from output and make evaluation possible.

misconceptions.mistake: Choosing a product before deciding what to learn.
misconceptions.correction: Make the product serve the learning goal.

misconceptions.mistake: Writing criteria after the product is finished.
misconceptions.correction: Freeze criteria early, then document justified changes.

practice.prompt: Distinguish a learning goal from a product goal using one example.
hints: Use “learn to” and “create”.
solution: Learning goal: learn to conduct oral-history interviews ethically.
Product goal: create a ten-minute edited audio documentary.

practice.prompt: Develop three success criteria for an illustrated beginner’s cooking guide.
hints: Include content, usability and testing.
solution: Examples: every recipe is tested twice; a beginner completes one recipe using only the guide; allergen information is visible for every recipe.

practice.prompt: A learner changes the project goal halfway through but has no dated record. Evaluate the evidence problem and recovery action.
hints: Separate the quality of the change from the missing trace.
solution: The change may be justified, but without dated evidence the reasoning and sequence cannot be established.
Reconstruct only from existing messages, drafts or files, label uncertainty, and document future decisions contemporaneously.

practice.prompt: Separate “Learn animation by making a two-minute film” into two goals.
hints: Identify the skill.
Identify the deliverable.
solution: Learning goal: develop skill in using timing to communicate movement.
Product goal: make a two-minute animated film within the available tools and time.
The film is evidence through which learning can be demonstrated, not the same thing as the learning itself.
successCriteria: Learning goal: develop skill in using timing to communicate movement.
Product goal: make a two-minute animated film within the available tools and time.
The film is evidence through which learning can be demonstrated, not the same thing as the learning itself.

practice.prompt: A learner promises a worldwide archive in two weeks with no contributors. Suggest a justified scope revision.
hints: Match ambition to resources.
Retain the core learning.
solution: Reduce the output to a small documented sample or prototype.
Keep the learning goal focused on organisation, research or presentation.
Record why limited time and access make the narrower scope more credible.
successCriteria: Reduce the output to a small documented sample or prototype.
Keep the learning goal focused on organisation, research or presentation.
Record why limited time and access make the narrower scope more credible.

checklist: My learning and product goals are distinct.
My process evidence records decisions when they happen.

notes.title: Goal development in context
paragraphs: A project goal should distinguish what you want to learn from what you plan to produce. A product can be completed without demonstrating the intended learning, and learning can occur even when a prototype remains incomplete. State a manageable skill or understanding, a reason it matters to you and a bounded output through which it can be explored. Check time, access and resources before promising an ambitious result. Keep the original goal visible when it changes, recording why the revision was necessary and what evidence will demonstrate progress.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional idea: “Make a website about local trees.” Develop a learning goal and a feasible product goal for a short school project.
steps: Learning goal: learn to organise and explain a small set of tree-identification features for beginners.
Product goal: create an offline prototype with six clearly labelled tree entries using permitted images or original drawings.
workedExamples.conclusion: The goals distinguish learning from output and bound the project without promising a complete botanical reference.

flashcards.front: How do learning and product goals differ?
flashcards.back: One concerns a skill or understanding; the other concerns the output.

flashcards.front: Why bound the scope?
flashcards.back: Time and access determine what can be completed credibly.

flashcards.front: Can an unfinished product still show learning?
flashcards.back: Yes, if the learning is evidenced and the product limit is reported honestly.

flashcards.front: What should a goal revision preserve?
flashcards.back: The earlier goal, reason for change and revised evidence plan.

diagrams.title: Goal development: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Interest → Learning goal → Product goal. The output provides a bounded way to apply that learning.

nodes.label: Interest
nodes.detail: Help beginners recognise local trees.

nodes.label: Learning goal
nodes.detail: Explain selected identification features clearly.

nodes.label: Product goal
nodes.detail: An offline six-entry prototype.

edges.label: The interest identifies a skill worth developing.
The output provides a bounded way to apply that learning.

lessons.summary: Build an ethical, answerable research plan that connects each question to a source method, quality check and project decision.
objectives: Prioritise research questions by decision value.
Match source methods to the evidence needed.
Record provenance, consent and uncertainty throughout the project.
keyIdeas: Research is useful when it changes or justifies a project decision.
Source quality depends on the question, method and context.
A clean evidence trail distinguishes what was found, inferred, created and revised.

definitions.meaning: A focused question whose answer informs the learning goal, product or evaluation.
Evidence collected directly for the project, such as an interview, observation, survey or test.
Comparing evidence from different methods or sources to test an interpretation.

method: List decisions the project must make.
Turn the riskiest unknowns into focused research questions.
Choose a source or method capable of answering each question.
Define credibility, consent, privacy and recording checks before collection.
Log findings separately from interpretations and link each decision to evidence.

workedExample.prompt: A learner is creating an accessible recipe guide for beginners.
steps: Decision: which instructions cause the most difficulty.
Secondary research can identify established readability and food-safety guidance.
Observed cooking trials can reveal where beginners hesitate or make errors.
Consent, allergy information and anonymised notes are planned before testing.
Revisions cite both guidance and observed task evidence.
workedExample.conclusion: The plan connects each research activity to a project decision instead of collecting information without purpose.

misconceptions.mistake: Counting sources instead of judging their use.
misconceptions.correction: Explain what each source can establish, its limits and which decision it informs.

misconceptions.mistake: Treating a search-result snippet as a source.
misconceptions.correction: Open the original material, record creator, title, date, publisher and stable location.

practice.prompt: Write two research questions for a project that creates a quiet study-space guide.
hints: One can address evidence; one can address users.
solution: What environmental features are associated with reduced distraction during independent study?
Which noise, lighting and seating problems do intended users report in the available spaces?

practice.prompt: Justify one secondary and one primary method for testing a beginner cycling-safety booklet.
hints: Connect each method to a decision.
solution: Current road-safety guidance can check factual rules and recommended behaviour.
A task-based comprehension test with intended readers can reveal unclear diagrams or instructions.
Together they test factual basis and usability.

practice.prompt: Ten friends praise a product concept in an informal poll. Evaluate what the evidence supports and plan a stronger next step.
hints: Consider sampling, question wording and behaviour.
solution: The poll suggests interest among a convenient social group but does not establish wider demand or successful use.
Record the questions and sample limits.
Recruit intended users beyond close friends and observe completion of representative tasks with a prototype.
Compare behaviour with stated preference before deciding.

practice.prompt: A project asks users whether they like a guide, then claims every fact is accurate. Evaluate.
hints: Preference and factual verification differ.
Name the missing check.
solution: User preference can inform presentation and perceived usefulness.
It does not verify factual claims.
Check those claims against suitable traceable sources or qualified review.
successCriteria: User preference can inform presentation and perceived usefulness.
It does not verify factual claims.
Check those claims against suitable traceable sources or qualified review.

practice.prompt: A research plan contains ten interesting questions unrelated to the product. How should they be prioritised?
hints: Return to the goal.
Identify decision-changing answers.
solution: Map each question to the learning goal or a product decision.
Prioritise questions whose answers affect accuracy, feasibility or user needs.
Set aside interesting but unrelated questions unless the project scope is deliberately revised.
successCriteria: Map each question to the learning goal or a product decision.
Prioritise questions whose answers affect accuracy, feasibility or user needs.
Set aside interesting but unrelated questions unless the project scope is deliberately revised.

checklist: My method can answer the question.
I preserve uncertainty and negative results.

notes.title: Research planning in context
paragraphs: Project research should answer questions that affect the learning goal or product decisions. Organise a plan around what needs to be known, where suitable evidence might be found and how its reliability will be judged. Different questions need different methods: a factual claim may require a traceable reference, while usability may require observation of intended users. Keep notes of sources and the decisions they inform. Agreement between copied sources is not independent confirmation. Collect only necessary personal information and use the school’s procedures for involving other people.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional project: a beginner guide to using a school telescope model. Identify two research questions without giving unsupervised equipment instructions.
steps: Ask which concepts beginners need to distinguish, using suitable educational references.
Ask whether the guide’s labels are understandable, using an approved classroom feedback task.
workedExamples.conclusion: The plan separates factual explanation from usability evidence and keeps actual equipment use within school guidance.

flashcards.front: What should a research question influence?
flashcards.back: A learning or product decision.

flashcards.front: Why use different methods?
flashcards.back: Factual accuracy and user experience require different evidence.

flashcards.front: What belongs in a source note?
flashcards.back: Origin, relevant claim, reliability considerations and the decision informed.

flashcards.front: Does repeated online agreement prove a claim?
flashcards.back: No; sources may copy the same unsupported account.

diagrams.title: Research planning: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Decision → Evidence methods → Use of findings. Each method informs the aspect it can actually test.

nodes.label: Decision
nodes.detail: What must a beginner guide explain?

nodes.label: Evidence methods
nodes.detail: Traceable references and approved user feedback.

nodes.label: Use of findings
nodes.detail: Revise content and labels for different reasons.

edges.label: The decision determines the research question.
Each method informs the aspect it can actually test.

lessons.summary: Use a contextual lens to connect a personal enquiry with people, places or systems while keeping the project’s practical scope manageable.
objectives: Explain why an enquiry matters in context.
Distinguish a broad connection from a manageable project.
Identify whose perspectives remain missing.
explanation: Context explains why a question matters and to whom, rather than adding a broad label to a finished product. A project about a local walking map could investigate how different people find their way through a shared place. That connection can guide choices about language, landmarks and access without requiring the learner to solve navigation for an entire city. Start with a genuine connection and name a question the project can actually explore.

A global perspective does not require making universal claims. Compare how circumstances might differ and identify the evidence needed before extending a local finding. This lesson develops the existing local topic map; it does not prescribe a current official project reporting requirement or reproduce a rubric. Confirm the framework and submission expectations used by your school. The original fictional cases below practise contextual reasoning, not proof that a real community has been consulted.
keyIdeas: A context shapes questions and choices.
Broad relevance can coexist with limited practical scope.
Local evidence does not automatically represent other settings.

definitions.meaning: A perspective used to connect an enquiry with relevant circumstances.
The people, setting, outcomes and limits included in a project.
A particular way of understanding an issue shaped by experience or position.

method: Describe the personal interest and relevant setting.
Identify a wider question the interest raises.
Select a feasible part to investigate.
Name missing perspectives and avoid extending claims beyond evidence.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional proposal: create a guide to quiet study spaces in one school. Explain a contextual connection without claiming to solve student wellbeing generally.
steps: Identify the local interest in finding a suitable study place.
Connect it to differences in how learners experience noise and shared space.
Limit the product to documented spaces and information within the school.
Seek appropriate, voluntary feedback without collecting private health details.
workedExample.conclusion: The project explores access to shared study space within a bounded setting; it does not establish a universal wellbeing intervention.

misconceptions.mistake: A context is only a label added to a title.
misconceptions.correction: Explain how it changes the enquiry or a product decision.

misconceptions.mistake: Global relevance means the product must serve everyone.
misconceptions.correction: Keep scope feasible and qualify the transfer of local findings.

practice.prompt: An original project makes a beginner guide to repairing a loose button. Explain one wider connection and one practical scope limit.
hints: Connect learning to an everyday practice.
solution: The enquiry can connect everyday repair with how people use and care for belongings.
Limit the guide to an appropriate simple task and intended audience; do not claim to solve all textile waste.

practice.prompt: A learner interviews three classmates about access to library books, then writes that all young people face the same barriers. Revise the contextual claim.
hints: Identify whose evidence is actually present.
solution: The interviews describe the experiences of those three classmates.
Use them to frame local questions, then seek other relevant perspectives before discussing wider patterns.
Do not replace missing evidence with an assumption that everyone shares the same circumstances.

practice.prompt: A learner adds “global sustainability” to a music-practice journal but makes no related research or design choices. How could the contextual connection become meaningful, or be revised?
hints: Do not force a label unrelated to the enquiry.
solution: Explain a genuine question that connects the project to the proposed context and identify evidence it needs.
If no such connection serves the learning goal, choose a more relevant lens with the supervisor rather than retaining a decorative label.
Record the reasoning and use the school’s current guidance.

practice.prompt: A learner says “My poster relates to the environment because it is green.” Improve the connection.
hints: Colour alone is superficial.
Name an issue and product decision.
solution: Identify a specific environmental question, such as explaining local reuse options.
Connect the poster’s information and audience to that question.
Explain what the poster can realistically inform rather than relying on its colour.
successCriteria: Identify a specific environmental question, such as explaining local reuse options.
Connect the poster’s information and audience to that question.
Explain what the poster can realistically inform rather than relying on its colour.

practice.prompt: A school-only survey is used to claim a worldwide trend. Explain the scope problem.
hints: Compare sample and population.
Keep the local finding.
solution: The evidence comes from one school.
It cannot establish a worldwide pattern without broader suitable data.
Report the local result and explain how it raises a wider question rather than claiming to answer that question globally.
successCriteria: The evidence comes from one school.
It cannot establish a worldwide pattern without broader suitable data.
Report the local result and explain how it raises a wider question rather than claiming to answer that question globally.

notes.title: Global context in context
paragraphs: A contextual connection explains why a project matters beyond the mechanics of making an object. It should be specific enough to guide inquiry, linking a personal interest with a social, cultural, environmental or other wider relationship. Avoid using a broad label as a substitute for explanation. A small project can explore a meaningful question without claiming to solve it at a global scale. Keep the connection consistent with the actual output and evidence. Use the school’s current project guidance when choosing any required formal context terminology.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional project: create a bilingual welcome map for one school club. Explain a bounded contextual connection.
steps: The project explores how language and information access affect newcomers’ participation.
The map can be tested with the club’s intended users, but its results do not establish a solution for every school or language community.
workedExamples.conclusion: The wider concern is inclusion through communication, explored through a specific local product.

flashcards.front: What makes a context connection meaningful?
flashcards.back: It explains a relationship that guides inquiry or product choices.

flashcards.front: Must a small project solve a global problem?
flashcards.back: No; it can explore a bounded part of a wider concern.

flashcards.front: Why avoid labels without explanation?
flashcards.back: A label alone does not show how the project relates to the context.

flashcards.front: What limits a project’s wider claims?
flashcards.back: Its actual scope, evidence and user setting.

diagrams.title: Global context: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Local product → Wider relationship → Bounded inquiry. The local scope defines what evidence can support.

nodes.label: Local product
nodes.detail: A bilingual club welcome map.

nodes.label: Wider relationship
nodes.detail: Language access and participation.

nodes.label: Bounded inquiry
nodes.detail: Test communication for this club’s newcomers.

edges.label: The product makes a broader issue concrete.
The local scope defines what evidence can support.

lessons.summary: Define what you intend to understand or become able to do and plan evidence that shows learning separately from completing an artefact.
objectives: Separate learning from product completion.
Identify a useful starting point.
Plan comparable evidence of developing skill.
explanation: A learning goal names a change in understanding or capability. “Make a website” specifies an output; “learn to organise information so a reader can find a named topic” identifies a capability that a website might help demonstrate. Choose a goal specific enough to investigate and feasible within the project’s resources. State what you already know so that later reflection can explain development rather than merely display a finished object.

Plan evidence appropriate to the goal. An early explanation, annotated attempt or decision record can show a starting point; later work can show what you can now do and why. A polished product created largely by someone else does not establish your own learning. Record assistance and source use, and distinguish an observed achievement from a future intention. These editorial exercises support planning; only your actual process and school assessment can establish what your project demonstrates.
keyIdeas: Learning is distinct from output.
A baseline helps explain change.
Assistance must remain visible in the evidence.

definitions.meaning: A specified understanding or capability the learner intends to develop.
Evidence of the starting knowledge or skill relevant to that goal.
Work or explanation that supports a claim about developing understanding or capability.

method: State the desired capability in clear language.
Describe relevant prior knowledge and limits.
Choose evidence that could demonstrate the capability.
Plan a later comparison and record help received.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional aim: “Make a short animation.” Develop a learning goal about communicating a movement through timing.
steps: Separate the film output from the skill of planning visual timing.
Propose learning to vary frame timing to communicate a selected movement clearly.
Keep an initial timing plan and later annotated versions explaining the changes.
Use feedback on the movement while recording which decisions the learner made.
workedExample.conclusion: The animation becomes evidence for learning about timing, rather than its existence being treated as proof of the skill.

misconceptions.mistake: A finished product automatically proves learning.
misconceptions.correction: Connect the claim to the learner’s decisions and understanding.

misconceptions.mistake: A learning goal must be impossibly ambitious to matter.
misconceptions.correction: Choose a meaningful challenge that is feasible and can be evidenced.

practice.prompt: Separate a learning goal and a product goal in an original proposal to make a beginner bird-identification booklet.
hints: What will the learner understand, and what will they make?
solution: Learning: develop the ability to compare relevant identifying features using reliable sources.
Product: a booklet for a specified beginner audience and bounded set of birds.

practice.prompt: A learner wants to improve explaining mathematical ideas visually. Propose baseline and later evidence without using a grade alone.
hints: Compare explanations and reasoning.
solution: Keep an initial original explanation and identify which relationships it makes clear or leaves ambiguous.
Create a later explanation with an annotated account of design decisions and appropriately gathered reader feedback.
Use comparable tasks and acknowledge differences in difficulty.

practice.prompt: A mentor rewrites most of a learner’s guide. The learner claims the final guide proves independent editing skill. Evaluate and suggest an honest evidence plan.
hints: Credit assistance and demonstrate personal decisions.
solution: Credit the mentor’s changes and do not treat them as independent learner performance.
Identify edits the learner can explain and compare a new bounded passage edited independently.
Record remaining difficulties rather than hiding the support received.

practice.prompt: Improve “I want to get better at photography” into a focused learning goal.
hints: Choose one controllable aspect.
Name evidence of development.
solution: A focused goal is to learn how framing changes emphasis in a portrait.
Create and compare several framing trials.
Explain the decisions using observations rather than relying only on which image is liked best.
successCriteria: A focused goal is to learn how framing changes emphasis in a portrait.
Create and compare several framing trials.
Explain the decisions using observations rather than relying only on which image is liked best.

practice.prompt: A learner says finishing a model proves improved research skills. What further evidence is needed?
hints: The output does not reveal the research process by itself.
Look for source evaluation and decisions.
solution: Show how sources were located and assessed.
Explain a decision changed by reliable evidence or a rejected weak source.
Compare this process with the starting approach to demonstrate learning.
successCriteria: Show how sources were located and assessed.
Explain a decision changed by reliable evidence or a rejected weak source.
Compare this process with the starting approach to demonstrate learning.

notes.title: Learning goal in context
paragraphs: A learning goal names a skill, understanding or process you intend to develop. Make it specific enough that evidence can show a change from the starting point. “Learn more” is too vague unless you explain what you will be able to do differently. A product provides opportunities to apply learning, but the learning evidence may include drafts, comparisons, explanations and revised decisions. Difficulty or failure can reveal learning when you analyse it honestly. Avoid defining success only as finishing, receiving praise or achieving a particular appearance.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional aim: “Make a podcast.” Refine the learning goal around interviewing.
steps: State the skill: learn to ask open questions and use follow-ups that respond to an interviewee’s answer.
Plan evidence: compare an early practice transcript with a later one and explain how the questions changed.
workedExamples.conclusion: The learning goal concerns responsive interviewing, while the podcast is the product through which it is practised.

flashcards.front: What should a learning goal name?
flashcards.back: A specific skill, understanding or process to develop.

flashcards.front: Why identify a starting point?
flashcards.back: It makes progress and change easier to demonstrate.

flashcards.front: What can evidence learning beyond a final product?
flashcards.back: Drafts, decisions, comparisons and explanations of revision.

flashcards.front: Can a failed attempt contribute evidence?
flashcards.back: Yes, when its lesson and resulting change are explained.

diagrams.title: Learning goal: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Starting point → Learning target → Evidence. The comparison can show how practice changed the skill.

nodes.label: Starting point
nodes.detail: Questions are mostly scripted and closed.

nodes.label: Learning target
nodes.detail: Use open questions and responsive follow-ups.

nodes.label: Evidence
nodes.detail: Compare early and later interview transcripts.

edges.label: The starting difficulty defines a meaningful skill target.
The comparison can show how practice changed the skill.

lessons.summary: Specify an achievable outcome with audience, purpose and boundaries so production decisions can be evaluated against a clear brief.
objectives: Describe the intended outcome.
Define audience and scope.
Distinguish necessary features from optional additions.
explanation: A product goal describes the outcome you intend to create or perform and the purpose it serves. Name its audience, form and practical boundaries. “A guide” is less useful than “a short illustrated guide that helps new club members find equipment and understand the borrowing routine”. Clear scope helps you choose which information and features are necessary, and gives later evaluation a stable reference point.

A product can support learning without including every possible feature. Balance available time, tools, access and review needs. If the scope changes, retain the original goal and explain the evidence behind the revision; do not silently redefine the product after a missed requirement. The hypothetical briefs here are practice cases, not completed real products. No audience testing or public release should be claimed from a written proposal alone, and school requirements remain authoritative for your submission.
keyIdeas: A goal includes purpose and audience.
Feasibility requires explicit boundaries.
Changes in scope need a traceable reason.

definitions.meaning: The intended artefact, performance or other outcome and its purpose.
The people for whom an outcome is intended.
A limit such as time, materials, permissions or access.

method: Identify the audience and task or experience.
Specify the form and essential content.
List practical constraints and exclusions.
Check alignment with learning and record justified changes.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional proposal: create an orientation guide for a school club with two weeks available and no access to a public website. Define a feasible product.
steps: Choose a locally shareable illustrated document for new members.
Include the meeting location, equipment routine and where to obtain current help.
Exclude online booking or a public portal that cannot be supported in the available setting.
Plan accuracy and readability checks before sharing through an approved school route.
workedExample.conclusion: The bounded document serves a clear audience and can be checked within the stated resources.

misconceptions.mistake: More features always make a stronger product.
misconceptions.correction: Features should serve the purpose and remain feasible.

misconceptions.mistake: A changed goal needs no record if the result looks good.
misconceptions.correction: Preserve the earlier scope and explain the revision.

practice.prompt: Improve “Create a podcast” by adding an audience, a purpose and one scope limit.
hints: Make the output understandable and feasible.
solution: Create a short original audio guide for new chess-club members explaining the meeting routine.
Limit it to orientation rather than claiming to teach all chess strategy; obtain appropriate access and review for any actual recording.

practice.prompt: An original fictional map project must show three accessible routes accurately. With limited time the learner wants to add animated icons before checking routes. Prioritise the work.
hints: Use the product’s core purpose.
solution: Check route accuracy and relevant access information first through appropriate current sources and review.
Animations are optional if they do not help the user find a route.
Do not claim verified accessibility from decorative presentation or an untested map.

practice.prompt: A learner planned a working prototype but produced only static screens. Explain how to report the outcome honestly and decide a next step.
hints: A screen image and working behaviour are different evidence.
solution: Report the static screens as a partial outcome and identify which behaviours remain unimplemented.
Evaluate the delivered material against the original criteria rather than silently calling it a working prototype.
Prioritise a small demonstrable interaction or document a justified scope revision with the supervisor.

practice.prompt: A product goal says “Create an app” with no users or features. Add the missing specificity using a fictional homework organiser.
hints: Name the audience.
Bound the functions.
solution: Create a clickable offline prototype for classmates to view and sort homework tasks.
Include task entry, due-date sorting and a completed-task view.
State that account syncing and notifications are outside the prototype scope.
successCriteria: Create a clickable offline prototype for classmates to view and sort homework tasks.
Include task entry, due-date sorting and a completed-task view.
State that account syncing and notifications are outside the prototype scope.

practice.prompt: A learner loses access to a required printer. How can the product goal be revised transparently?
hints: Preserve the original goal.
Change the deliverable to match access.
solution: Record the loss of printing access.
Revise the product to a print-ready digital file or another feasible format.
Update the criteria and explain what can and cannot now be tested.
successCriteria: Record the loss of printing access.
Revise the product to a print-ready digital file or another feasible format.
Update the criteria and explain what can and cannot now be tested.

checklist: I report the delivered outcome accurately.

notes.title: Product goal in context
paragraphs: A product goal defines what will be made, for whom and within what boundaries. Specify a form and scope that can be delivered with available time, materials and permissions. A prototype can be an appropriate product when it is clearly labelled and evaluated as a prototype. Do not promise live features that depend on services or contributors you cannot access. Separate essential functions from desirable extras. This makes later decisions about scope transparent and helps evaluators judge the intended outcome rather than an imagined larger version.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional project: a learner has ten days and can use only offline tools. Define a feasible guide for new chess-club members.
steps: Choose an offline six-page illustrated guide with meeting information, equipment labels and three beginner activities.
State that it is a printable draft for the school club, with factual and usability checks planned before use.
workedExamples.conclusion: The output is concrete and bounded; a live registration service is outside the available resources.

flashcards.front: What should a product goal identify?
flashcards.back: The output, audience, scope and relevant constraints.

flashcards.front: Can a prototype be a legitimate outcome?
flashcards.back: Yes, if its status and evaluation limits are explicit.

flashcards.front: Why separate essential and optional features?
flashcards.back: It supports realistic prioritisation when resources are limited.

flashcards.front: What makes an external dependency risky for scope?
flashcards.back: Its availability may be outside the learner’s control.

diagrams.title: Product goal: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Constraints → Essential output → Boundary. The defined scope prevents unplanned dependency promises.

nodes.label: Constraints
nodes.detail: Ten days and offline tools.

nodes.label: Essential output
nodes.detail: A six-page beginner guide.

nodes.label: Boundary
nodes.detail: No live registration or unsupported service claims.

edges.label: The constraints shape a feasible format.
The defined scope prevents unplanned dependency promises.

lessons.summary: Define observable quality criteria and matching evidence before judging a product, while preserving unmet requirements and the limits of a small test.
objectives: Write clear product criteria.
Match each criterion to a suitable check.
Evaluate results without moving the goalposts.
explanation: Success criteria describe qualities an outcome should demonstrate, and a check specifies how you will examine them. Separate a requirement from an activity: “interview three people” is a process task, while “readers can locate the three named sections without help” describes a product outcome. Use meaningful qualitative or quantitative evidence, depending on the quality being judged. Numbers alone do not make an irrelevant criterion useful.

Define the conditions and any threshold before testing. Record which version was tested, who or what was included, and what counts as assistance or failure. A small trial can guide revision without certifying all users. If new evidence justifies changing a criterion, date and explain the change rather than lowering a target after seeing an unwanted result. These fictional checks are editorial practice examples, not an official project rubric or a substitute for teacher assessment.
keyIdeas: Criteria describe outcome quality.
Tests need conditions and a version.
An unmet requirement remains visible even when other criteria pass.

definitions.meaning: An explicit quality used to judge the intended outcome.
A specified boundary used to interpret a check.
The circumstances under which evidence is collected.

method: State the relevant product quality.
Define the version, conditions and any threshold.
Collect and classify evidence consistently.
Judge each criterion and retain unmet requirements.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional criterion: at least four of five beginner readers must find the emergency contact section without hints. In the supplied trial three do so alone, one needs a hint, and one cannot find it. Judge the criterion.
steps: Identify independent completion as the stated condition.
Count three independent successes, not four.
Compare three with the predeclared threshold of four.
Record the criterion as unmet and inspect the navigation before retesting a named version.
workedExample.conclusion: The trial does not meet the criterion; the assisted attempt remains useful evidence but is not an independent success.

misconceptions.mistake: A positive comment proves every criterion is met.
misconceptions.correction: Match evidence separately to each criterion.

misconceptions.mistake: Changing a threshold after a failure preserves the original pass claim.
misconceptions.correction: Keep the original result and justify any later revised criterion separately.

practice.prompt: Rewrite “The booklet must be good” as one observable criterion and a matching check.
hints: Choose a quality relevant to its audience.
solution: The intended beginner readers can locate the contents page and identify the section for a specified task without hints.
Use a predeclared task and record version, participants and any assistance.

practice.prompt: Original fictional threshold: at least 80% of ten readers must complete a task unaided. Seven do, two complete it with help and one does not. Calculate the independent completion rate and judge the threshold.
hints: Use the full stated denominator and exclude assisted success.
solution: Independent completion = 7 / 10 × 100 = 70%.
70% is below 80%, so the criterion is unmet; retain the two assisted completions as separate evidence.

practice.prompt: A product passes four visual criteria but fails a mandatory factual-accuracy check. The learner claims four out of five means it is ready to share. Evaluate.
hints: A mandatory gate is not cancelled by unrelated passes.
solution: Preserve the four supported visual results, but the mandatory accuracy condition remains unmet.
Correct and verify the factual issue on the relevant version before claiming readiness.
Do not use an average pass count to hide a required failure.

practice.prompt: A criterion requires all eight links to work; seven work. Evaluate the result.
hints: Use the stated standard.
Do not round it into a pass.
solution: Seven of eight links work.
The criterion requires all eight.
The criterion is not met until the remaining link is repaired and checked.
successCriteria: The criterion is not met until the remaining link is repaired and checked.

practice.prompt: A learner changes “five of six” to “four of six” after four succeed, with no new justification. Explain the problem.
hints: The result influenced the threshold.
Preserve honest evaluation.
solution: The threshold is being altered to fit the outcome.
That undermines the original test of success.
Report the original criterion as unmet and justify any future revision independently before retesting.
successCriteria: The threshold is being altered to fit the outcome.
That undermines the original test of success.
Report the original criterion as unmet and justify any future revision independently before retesting.

checklist: I bind results to a version.

notes.title: Success criteria in context
paragraphs: Success criteria turn a product goal into standards that can be evaluated. Define the feature, threshold and evidence method before testing. Some criteria concern measurable performance; others require a reasoned qualitative judgement. Keep critical factual or safety requirements separate from preferences so a high average cannot hide a serious failure. Criteria should be feasible to test with the available users and resources. If a criterion changes, preserve the earlier version and explain why; do not lower a threshold after seeing results merely to claim success.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional guide criterion: at least five of six first-time readers locate the meeting place within 20 seconds without hints. Results: 12, 18, 24, 15, 19 and 17 seconds; the 15-second attempt used a hint.
steps: Unaided successes are 12, 18, 19 and 17 seconds: four readers.
The 24-second attempt exceeds the limit and the hinted attempt fails the unaided condition.
workedExamples.conclusion: The criterion is not met: four of six is below the required five.

flashcards.front: When should criteria be set?
flashcards.back: Before collecting the results used to judge them.

flashcards.front: What makes a criterion testable?
flashcards.back: A defined feature or task, standard and evidence method.

flashcards.front: Can preference scores cancel a critical factual error?
flashcards.back: No; critical requirements need separate judgement.

flashcards.front: How should changed criteria be recorded?
flashcards.back: Preserve the prior version and explain the reason for revision.

diagrams.title: Success criteria: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Criterion → Evidence → Judgement. The valid count is compared with the pre-set threshold.

nodes.label: Criterion
nodes.detail: Five of six readers, within 20 seconds, no hints.

nodes.label: Evidence
nodes.detail: Four attempts satisfy all conditions.

nodes.label: Judgement
nodes.detail: The threshold is not met.

edges.label: Each attempt is classified using every condition.
The valid count is compared with the pre-set threshold.

lessons.summary: Explain how a specific learning strategy supported a project decision, using evidence rather than merely naming a skill category.
objectives: Recognise the five broad ATL categories.
Connect a strategy to a task and evidence.
Evaluate what helped and what still needs development.
explanation: Approaches to learning include communication, social, self-management, research and thinking skills across IB programmes. Naming a category does not show how you used it. Explain the task, the strategy and the evidence of its effect. For example, a source-comparison table can support research and thinking when it helps distinguish a documented fact from a repeated unsupported claim; an unused table proves little by itself.

Choose examples relevant to your learning goal and product rather than trying to force every category into every activity. A strategy may help one part of a task while leaving another unresolved. Record assistance, adaptation and unsuccessful attempts so that the account remains credible. The original fictional cases here illustrate skill use; they are not official descriptors, an exhaustive skill framework or claims about your actual project. Follow your school’s current reporting guidance when selecting evidence.
keyIdeas: A category is not evidence of application.
Explain the strategy’s role in a decision.
Effective self-management includes adapting a plan.

definitions.meaning: A deliberate approach used to address a learning or project task.
Managing time, organisation and responses to demands in a learning process.
Applying a learned strategy in a different relevant situation.

method: Identify the task and difficulty.
Name the strategy and relevant skill category.
Show the evidence of how the strategy was used.
Evaluate its contribution and a remaining development need.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional record: a learner compared the authors, dates and evidence of three sources. Two repeated the same uncited claim; one provided a traceable explanation. Show how ATL skills informed a decision.
steps: Identify source evaluation as the research task.
Describe comparison and checking as research and thinking strategies.
Explain why repeated unsupported claims were not counted as independent confirmation.
Record which product statement was revised and which uncertainty remained.
workedExample.conclusion: The account demonstrates a strategy affecting a decision, rather than simply asserting “I used research skills”.

misconceptions.mistake: A checklist tick proves a skill was applied well.
misconceptions.correction: Use a specific action, artefact and consequence.

misconceptions.mistake: A strategy works equally well in every setting.
misconceptions.correction: Consider context and adapt it when the evidence shows a limitation.

practice.prompt: Improve “I used communication skills” using an original example where a learner rewrote an unclear interview question before asking it.
hints: Name the action and its purpose.
solution: The learner replaced ambiguous wording with a clear question about one topic.
This applied communication skills to help participants understand the question; actual response evidence is still needed to judge whether it worked.

practice.prompt: A fictional project plan had dates but no time for feedback. The learner added a review milestone and revised a section before completion. Explain relevant skill use.
hints: A plan can be improved in response to a problem.
solution: Self-management was applied by making review time explicit rather than only listing production dates.
Thinking and communication may support interpreting feedback, but the account should name the actual action and evidence.
The revision record can show how the milestone affected the outcome.

practice.prompt: A learner says group feedback proves social skills but interrupted every contributor and kept no record of suggestions. Evaluate the evidence and propose a better approach.
hints: Attendance is not the same as effective collaboration.
solution: Participating in a group does not by itself demonstrate effective social skills.
Use agreed turn-taking, record suggestions accurately and explain how decisions considered different contributions.
Reflect honestly on the earlier limitation rather than inventing positive feedback.

practice.prompt: A learner claims collaboration because several people were in the room. What evidence would strengthen the claim?
hints: Presence is not a collaborative action.
Look for shared decisions and responses.
solution: Record a specific contribution or exchange.
Explain how participants negotiated or combined ideas.
Show how that interaction changed the work or resolved a problem.
successCriteria: Record a specific contribution or exchange.
Explain how participants negotiated or combined ideas.
Show how that interaction changed the work or resolved a problem.

practice.prompt: A timetable is missed, then revised using actual task durations. Explain a self-management learning point.
hints: Use the difference between estimate and evidence.
Describe the adjustment.
solution: The learner recognises that the original estimates were inaccurate.
Recorded durations support a more realistic revised plan.
The learning lies in monitoring and adapting, not pretending the first schedule was followed.
successCriteria: The learner recognises that the original estimates were inaccurate.
Recorded durations support a more realistic revised plan.
The learning lies in monitoring and adapting, not pretending the first schedule was followed.

checklist: I link it to a decision.

notes.title: ATL skills in context
paragraphs: Approaches to learning are demonstrated through purposeful actions, not by attaching skill names to a finished product. Show the situation, the strategy used and its effect on the project. Research skill can appear in checking a source’s origin; communication skill can appear in revising an explanation after reader feedback. Self-management includes monitoring a plan and adapting when evidence shows it is unrealistic. Select a few strong examples and explain them with records. A claim such as “I used critical thinking” needs a concrete decision to make it assessable.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional record: a learner finds two contradictory dates for an event, checks the cited archive and corrects the guide. Explain the learning skill.
steps: The learner identifies a conflict rather than choosing the more convenient date.
Tracing the archive and revising the guide demonstrates source evaluation and evidence-based decision-making.
workedExamples.conclusion: The skill claim is supported by the conflicting notes, checked source and recorded correction.

flashcards.front: What makes a skill claim convincing?
flashcards.back: A concrete situation, action, evidence and effect.

flashcards.front: How can communication skill be evidenced?
flashcards.back: Show how an explanation changed in response to a reader’s need or feedback.

flashcards.front: What is more useful than listing many skills?
flashcards.back: A few well-explained examples linked to the project.

flashcards.front: How can self-management include revision?
flashcards.back: Monitoring progress can justify changing an unrealistic plan.

diagrams.title: ATL skills: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Challenge → Strategy → Effect. The checked evidence changes the product decision.

nodes.label: Challenge
nodes.detail: Two sources give different dates.

nodes.label: Strategy
nodes.detail: Trace the original evidence.

nodes.label: Effect
nodes.detail: Correct the guide and record the reason.

edges.label: The conflict creates a need for source evaluation.
The checked evidence changes the product decision.

lessons.summary: Keep a dated evidence trail that distinguishes sources, original work, assistance, feedback and changes without inventing a smooth project history.
objectives: Bind evidence to dates and versions.
Record assistance and source use.
Preserve changes and missing evidence honestly.
explanation: A process record explains how decisions developed. Label drafts and tests with a date or version, identify relevant sources, and state why a change was made. Keep observations separate from interpretation: “two readers looked in the wrong section” is a finding; “the heading may be ambiguous” is a possible explanation. Link the eventual revision to the evidence that motivated it, rather than claiming that every change was planned from the start.

Documentation should preserve setbacks and assistance as well as achievements. Retain earlier versions when feasible, mark later recollections as retrospective, and avoid adding invented meetings or test results to fill gaps. Collect only appropriate information, use consent where required and keep personal details out of unnecessary shared records. The fictional project records used here are practice material; completing an answer does not create a verified process portfolio or replace the school’s actual submission requirements.
keyIdeas: An evidence trail connects decisions to their basis.
Versions prevent results being assigned to the wrong product.
Honest gaps are better than fabricated completeness.

definitions.meaning: Dated evidence and explanation of project activity, decisions and development.
Identification of the source or contributor responsible for material or assistance.
An identifiable state of an artefact at a particular stage.

method: Identify the date, version and decision.
Record relevant evidence and its source.
Explain the decision and any assistance.
Retain earlier results and label uncertainties or later recollections.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional log: v1 readers missed the contents link; v2 moved it; no retest has occurred. Write a traceable progress entry.
steps: Identify the v1 finding and its original test context.
Record the location change as a v2 design decision.
State that the change is intended to improve discovery, not that it has already succeeded.
Schedule an appropriate v2 check and keep the v1 result.
workedExample.conclusion: The entry records a completed change and a pending test without converting intention into an observed outcome.

misconceptions.mistake: A final screenshot shows the entire process.
misconceptions.correction: Use selected earlier evidence and explain the decisions between versions.

misconceptions.mistake: Missing notes justify reconstructing exact invented results.
misconceptions.correction: Label recollection and acknowledge unavailable evidence.

practice.prompt: Classify these original fictional notes: “Three users asked where to start”; “the heading may be unclear”; “rename the heading in v2”.
hints: Separate evidence, explanation and action.
solution: The first is an observation within the stated trial.
The second is a hypothesis about its cause.
The third is a proposed revision, whose effect needs checking.

practice.prompt: A mentor suggests an outline, but the learner writes and revises the actual text. How should the process record describe contributions?
hints: Credit help without erasing the learner’s work.
solution: Attribute the outline suggestion to the mentor.
Identify the learner’s drafting and specific revisions with versions or examples.
Explain how the suggestion influenced the work without claiming either complete independence or that the mentor wrote the whole product.

practice.prompt: A learner has no notes from a first feedback meeting and wants to insert exact positive quotations remembered weeks later. Suggest an honest alternative.
hints: Memory is not a verbatim transcript.
solution: Label any recollection as retrospective and avoid quotation marks for uncertain wording.
Use surviving drafts or messages where appropriate to support what can be checked.
Acknowledge gaps and improve documentation for later meetings without inventing the missing record.

practice.prompt: A log says “Test passed” but contains only a test plan. Correct the status.
hints: Identify what has actually happened.
Keep the next action clear.
solution: The test is planned, not completed.
No pass or fail result is yet supported.
Record the procedure and schedule the test, then attach actual observations before judging the outcome.
successCriteria: The test is planned, not completed.
No pass or fail result is yet supported.
Record the procedure and schedule the test, then attach actual observations before judging the outcome.

practice.prompt: A source claim is corrected late in the project. What should documentation preserve?
hints: Keep the error trace without repeating it as current fact.
Link the replacement to evidence.
solution: Identify the earlier claim as superseded.
Record the reliable evidence supporting the correction.
List the affected product sections and confirm which were updated.
successCriteria: Identify the earlier claim as superseded.
Record the reliable evidence supporting the correction.
List the affected product sections and confirm which were updated.

notes.title: Process documentation in context
paragraphs: Project documentation should preserve the chain from intention to action, evidence and decision. Date or version important records and identify what actually happened. A planned test and a completed test are different kinds of evidence; label them clearly. Keep corrections visible so a later reader can understand the development rather than seeing a polished reconstruction. Store source references near the claims they support. Choose useful evidence rather than collecting every screenshot: the record should make decisions explainable and distinguish completed, incomplete and unresolved work.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional log: version 1 has a confusing contents page; version 2 adds page numbers, but no reader has tested it. Write an accurate progress entry.
steps: Record the observed v1 problem and the v2 change.
State that improved navigation is an expectation, with a reader test still pending.
workedExamples.conclusion: The entry documents a completed revision without mislabelling it as a proven improvement.

flashcards.front: Why distinguish planned and completed tests?
flashcards.back: A plan does not supply outcome evidence.

flashcards.front: What makes a revision trace useful?
flashcards.back: It shows what changed, why and what evidence followed.

flashcards.front: Should corrections erase earlier claims?
flashcards.back: No; preserve enough history to explain the correction.

flashcards.front: What evidence should be retained?
flashcards.back: Records that support significant decisions, learning and evaluation.

diagrams.title: Process documentation: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Observed issue → Completed action → Pending evidence. The revision creates a hypothesis that still needs checking.

nodes.label: Observed issue
nodes.detail: Readers struggle with the contents page.

nodes.label: Completed action
nodes.detail: Page numbers are added in v2.

nodes.label: Pending evidence
nodes.detail: A new reader test has not occurred.

edges.label: The issue justifies the revision.
The revision creates a hypothesis that still needs checking.

lessons.summary: Use project evidence to explain changes in understanding, skill and decision-making without confusing effort, product quality and learning.
objectives: Select a significant learning episode.
Explain how evidence changed a decision.
Identify a transferable next step with limits.
explanation: Reflection explains what an experience changed in your understanding and why. A chronological account can locate events, but a useful reflection selects an important decision, its evidence and the learning it produced. A product that missed a criterion can still reveal genuine learning about planning or source evaluation. Conversely, completing an attractive product does not by itself explain what the learner now understands or can do independently.

Connect claims to actual work and retain uncertainty. Compare a starting attempt with a later explanation, or show how contradictory evidence changed a decision. State which help was needed and where the strategy might transfer next. Do not turn a hypothetical future action into a completed achievement. These fictional exercises provide practice in evidence-based reflection; they do not report your experience, certify personal growth or supply official assessed reflections for submission.
keyIdeas: Learning and product quality are related but distinct.
A setback can support learning without becoming a product success.
Transfer is a claim that needs an appropriate new context.

definitions.meaning: An explanation of learning from experience and evidence that informs future action.
A new or revised understanding supported by the learner’s experience.
A boundary on what the available evidence supports.

method: Select an episode connected to the learning goal.
Identify evidence and the original assumption.
Explain what changed in understanding or strategy.
State a realistic next application and its limits.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional case: a learner trusted three websites because they agreed, then discovered all repeated one uncited story. Reflect on the learning rather than claiming the product was already accurate.
steps: State the initial assumption that repeated agreement meant independent support.
Identify the discovery of a common unsupported origin.
Explain learning to examine provenance and independence.
Revise affected claims and use source tracing in a later enquiry; accuracy still needs checking.
workedExample.conclusion: The episode supports a specific change in research understanding, while the product’s factual repair remains a separate task.

misconceptions.mistake: Reflection must describe uninterrupted improvement.
misconceptions.correction: Explain setbacks and unresolved difficulties honestly.

misconceptions.mistake: Feeling proud proves the learning goal was achieved.
misconceptions.correction: Use concrete evidence alongside personal responses.

practice.prompt: Explain the difference between “I worked for five hours” and an evidence-based reflection about managing work.
hints: Time spent is an activity measure.
solution: Five hours records effort but does not explain strategy or learning.
A reflection could show how breaking a task into milestones exposed a missing review step and changed the next plan.

practice.prompt: An original fictional prototype failed a navigation check. The learner identified a misleading label and can explain why it confused readers, but has not retested. Write a bounded reflection.
hints: Learning can occur before the product passes.
solution: The failure helped the learner recognise the difference between a label familiar to the maker and one clear to intended readers.
That supports learning about audience-centred wording.
The proposed revision’s effectiveness remains unverified until a suitable retest.

practice.prompt: A learner claims “I can now manage any project” after finishing one small booklet with substantial supervisor support. Revise the claim and propose evidence for transfer.
hints: Preserve achievement and its actual scope.
solution: Describe the particular planning strategies used on the booklet and acknowledge supervisor support.
Avoid extending one outcome to every project.
Apply a selected strategy to a new bounded task, recording what can be done independently and what needs adaptation.

practice.prompt: A reflection says “I became a perfect researcher”. Improve it using evidence of one source-checking skill.
hints: Narrow the claim.
Describe a demonstrated change.
solution: State that the learner improved at tracing claims to their original source.
Give an example of rejecting a copied unsupported claim.
Acknowledge remaining skills to develop rather than claiming perfection.
successCriteria: State that the learner improved at tracing claims to their original source.
Give an example of rejecting a copied unsupported claim.
Acknowledge remaining skills to develop rather than claiming perfection.

practice.prompt: A project prototype remains unfinished, but the learner can now explain and apply a new modelling method. How should reflection separate outcomes?
hints: Report both product and learning status.
Use evidence for each.
solution: State clearly which product features remain incomplete.
Demonstrate the modelling method through worked trials or explanations.
Conclude that learning occurred while the full product goal was not yet met.
successCriteria: State clearly which product features remain incomplete.
Demonstrate the modelling method through worked trials or explanations.
Conclude that learning occurred while the full product goal was not yet met.

checklist: I connect reflection to a goal.
I distinguish learning from product success.

notes.title: Reflection in context
paragraphs: Project reflection explains how the work changed your understanding, strategies or perspective. Choose a significant experience and connect it to evidence of learning. Difficulty alone is not a reflection; explain what you learned from it and how your later approach changed. Avoid claiming personal transformation without examples. A product limitation can still reveal a valuable learning outcome, while a successful product does not automatically prove every intended skill improved. Distinguish the project’s effects on your own learning from wider impacts that have not been measured.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional case: early instructions used unexplained abbreviations. After beginner feedback, the learner rewrote them and tested the revision. Reflect on communication learning.
steps: The feedback challenges the assumption that familiar terms are familiar to every reader.
The revision demonstrates a shift towards defining terms and checking understanding with the intended audience.
workedExamples.conclusion: The learning concerns adapting explanation to readers, supported by the before-and-after text and feedback.

flashcards.front: What should reflection connect?
flashcards.back: An experience, evidence of learning and a change in understanding or action.

flashcards.front: Can a limitation support learning?
flashcards.back: Yes, if the learner explains what it revealed and how they responded.

flashcards.front: Why avoid unmeasured impact claims?
flashcards.back: The project may not contain evidence about wider effects.

flashcards.front: What distinguishes learning from completion?
flashcards.back: Learning concerns changed capability or understanding, not merely finishing an output.

diagrams.title: Reflection: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Assumption → Feedback → Learning. The mismatch changes the learner’s communication strategy.

nodes.label: Assumption
nodes.detail: Readers know the abbreviations.

nodes.label: Feedback
nodes.detail: Beginners cannot follow the instructions.

nodes.label: Learning
nodes.detail: Explain terms and test understanding.

edges.label: The feedback reveals a mismatch in assumed knowledge.
The mismatch changes the learner’s communication strategy.

lessons.summary: Evaluate a delivered product criterion by criterion, distinguish its quality from personal learning, and report incomplete evidence without disguising it as success.
objectives: Match results to predeclared criteria.
Distinguish pass, unmet and untested conditions.
Prioritise a justified next revision.
explanation: Product evaluation compares the delivered version with the criteria established for it. Identify the evidence used for each judgement and distinguish “met”, “not met” and “not yet tested”. A missing test is not a pass, and positive appearance feedback cannot substitute for factual accuracy or functional evidence. If a criterion was revised, preserve its earlier form and explain which version of the criterion and product a judgement concerns.

Evaluate learning separately using the process evidence relevant to the learning goal. A partial product may accompany meaningful learning, but that does not justify claiming unfinished features work. Describe the intended audience, sample and conditions behind any test result, then choose the next revision by relevance rather than convenience. These original fictional cases practise transparent evaluation; their editorial criteria are not an official marking rubric or approval for a real release or submission.
keyIdeas: Judgements need matching evidence.
Untested is different from passed.
Learning claims and product claims require their own support.

definitions.meaning: A record linking each criterion to evidence, judgement and limitations.
A condition for which the required evidence has not been collected.
A change selected because it addresses an important evidenced limitation.

method: Identify the delivered version and agreed criteria.
Match appropriate evidence to each criterion.
Classify supported, unmet and untested conditions.
Separate learning evidence and prioritise the next revision.

workedExample.prompt: Original fictional guide: layout passes the agreed reading check; one safety instruction is inaccurate; translation has not been reviewed. Evaluate readiness without averaging these conditions.
steps: Record layout as supported by its specific check.
Record the inaccurate instruction as an unmet requirement.
Record translation as untested, not passed.
Prioritise correcting and checking the instruction and obtaining appropriate translation review before any readiness claim.
workedExample.conclusion: The evidence supports a mixed, incomplete product evaluation; the successful layout does not cancel the other conditions.

misconceptions.mistake: Untested means probably successful.
misconceptions.correction: Report it as unknown until appropriate evidence exists.

misconceptions.mistake: A high average score cancels a mandatory failure.
misconceptions.correction: Respect required conditions and report them separately.

practice.prompt: Original fictional results: a booklet includes all planned sections; its links were not checked; one diagram has a wrong label. Classify the three conditions and propose a correction for any unmet condition.
hints: Use met, untested and not met appropriately.
solution: Section inclusion is met on the supplied evidence.
Link functionality is untested.
Diagram accuracy is not met; correct and verify the label.

practice.prompt: A product passes a task with four friends who already know the layout. The criterion concerns first-time users. Explain the evidence limit and next check.
hints: Prior familiarity changes the test population.
solution: The result supports completion by those familiar participants under the supplied conditions.
It does not establish the first-time-user criterion.
Use appropriate unfamiliar intended readers and the predeclared unaided task, recording any help and failures.

practice.prompt: An original fictional project met its visual criteria but missed its core search function. The learner learned substantial layout skills and asks to call the whole project fully successful. Give a balanced evaluation.
hints: Keep learning and product judgements separate.
solution: Recognise evidenced layout learning and the visual criteria that were met.
Report the missing search function as an unmet product requirement, not erased by those achievements.
Prioritise a bounded working search or document the partial outcome and justified future work without inventing a pass.

practice.prompt: A product meets four optional preferences but fails one mandatory access requirement. Evaluate.
hints: Do not count criteria as equal votes.
Use their stated importance.
solution: The four preferences are genuine strengths.
The mandatory access requirement remains unmet.
The product cannot be judged fully successful under that specification until the access issue is resolved.
successCriteria: The four preferences are genuine strengths.
The mandatory access requirement remains unmet.
The product cannot be judged fully successful under that specification until the access issue is resolved.

practice.prompt: A learner claims all users will understand a guide after testing two friends. Explain a better conclusion.
hints: Name the actual tested group.
State the limit and next evidence.
solution: The two friends understood it under the trial conditions.
That does not establish understanding for all intended users.
Test a more relevant range of first-time users and report the remaining limits.
successCriteria: The two friends understood it under the trial conditions.
That does not establish understanding for all intended users.
Test a more relevant range of first-time users and report the remaining limits.

checklist: I separate learning and product evidence.
I prioritise the relevant next revision.

notes.title: Evaluation in context
paragraphs: Product evaluation uses the agreed criteria and actual evidence to judge what the output achieves. Report met, unmet and untested criteria separately. A critical error should not disappear inside an average score, and a visually attractive result can still fail an information requirement. Explain the scope of trials and whether participants represent the intended audience. Improvements should address specific findings. Keep evaluation distinct from reflection: evaluation judges the product against standards, while reflection explains what the learner gained from the process.

workedExamples.prompt: Original fictional guide: layout meets the readability trial, two dates are wrong, and one translated section has not been checked. Evaluate readiness.
steps: The layout has supporting evidence, but factual accuracy fails for the two dates.
The translation criterion remains untested rather than passed.
workedExamples.conclusion: The guide is not ready under criteria requiring accurate dates and checked translations; correct and verify those parts before reassessing.

flashcards.front: How does evaluation differ from reflection?
flashcards.back: Evaluation judges the product; reflection explains learning from the process.

flashcards.front: What does untested mean?
flashcards.back: There is insufficient evidence to judge a criterion.

flashcards.front: Can appearance compensate for factual error?
flashcards.back: No, when factual accuracy is a required criterion.

flashcards.front: What should an improvement proposal reference?
flashcards.back: A specific failed or uncertain criterion and the evidence behind it.

diagrams.title: Evaluation: relationships to explain
diagrams.description: Evidence → Separate judgements → Next action. The unresolved requirements determine readiness.

nodes.label: Evidence
nodes.detail: Layout passes, dates fail, translation is unchecked.

nodes.label: Separate judgements
nodes.detail: Met, unmet and untested criteria remain distinct.

nodes.label: Next action
nodes.detail: Correct dates and review translation before reassessment.

edges.label: Different evidence supports different criterion statuses.
The unresolved requirements determine readiness.
